oneSentence: A structured collection of texts or speech transcripts used to study language or train and test language-processing systems.
plainExplanation:
A corpus is a body of language data gathered for a purpose. It usually contains many documents, sentences, or transcripts collected in one place. The items may be books, news articles, call-centre transcripts, social media posts, parliamentary debates, or transcribed speech.

What goes in depends on the task. For machine translation, a corpus may contain sentence pairs in two languages. For sentiment analysis, it may contain reviews labelled positive or negative. For named-entity recognition, it may contain text where names of people, places, and organisations have been marked.

What happens next is preparation. The text is cleaned, organised, and often annotated, meaning humans or software add useful labels or structure. Researchers or developers then use the corpus to analyse patterns in language, train a model, or test whether a system works well on the kind of language it will meet in practice.

What comes out is not the corpus itself, but evidence or a system built from it. For example, a corpus can reveal which words often appear together, help train a translation system, or show that a chatbot performs poorly on a regional variety of English. A corpus is related to a dataset, but it usually refers specifically to language material rather than any kind of data.

everydayAnalogy.title: Planning a journey with many travellers' notes
everydayAnalogy.story: Imagine a team in Nairobi, São Paulo and Bangkok trying to make a better city journey guide. They collect thousands of past traveller notes: short messages about delays, station names, transfer times and common questions. They sort the notes by route, language and topic, and mark some with labels such as “late bus” or “ticket problem”. Then they use that organised collection to spot patterns and improve the guide.

everydayAnalogy.limitation: A real corpus is usually much larger and more formally structured than a pile of traveller notes. It may include millions of words, careful sampling rules, tokenisation or other processing steps, and quality checks. Also, a corpus does not by itself “improve” a system; people and algorithms use it for analysis, training or evaluation.

visual.title: How a corpus is built and used
visual.learningObjective: Show that a corpus is language material collected, organised and often labelled so it can support analysis, training or evaluation.
visual.description: A left-to-right flow with four boxes. Read from source texts, to collection, to preparation, to use. Small examples in each box show how raw language becomes an organised resource for a specific task.

steps.label: 1. Source texts
steps.explanation: Start with language materials such as articles, reports, transcripts or message logs collected for a defined purpose.
steps.visualInstruction: Draw a box with document and speech-bubble icons labelled “articles”, “transcripts”, “messages”. Add a caption: “Raw language material”.

steps.label: 2. Gather into one collection
steps.explanation: Bring the texts together and record basic information such as language, date, source or domain.
steps.visualInstruction: Draw arrows from the source box into a larger container labelled “Corpus”. Add small tags: “language”, “date”, “source”.

steps.label: 3. Clean and annotate
steps.explanation: Remove obvious errors where needed and add labels or markup if the task requires them, such as sentiment labels or named entities.
steps.visualInstruction: Show the corpus box leading to a second corpus box with coloured highlights and tag labels like “positive” and “organisation”.

steps.label: 4. Use for a task
steps.explanation: The organised corpus can then support language analysis, model training, or testing whether a system works on relevant text.
steps.visualInstruction: Draw three outgoing arrows to small boxes labelled “analyse”, “train”, and “test” with example outputs like a chart, a model icon, and an evaluation score.

visual.interaction: Hover or tap each stage to reveal a short example, such as a raw sentence becoming a labelled sentence for named-entity recognition.
visual.accessibilityDescription: The diagram is a four-step flow from left to right. Step 1 shows raw language sources such as articles, transcripts and messages. Step 2 shows these gathered into a single corpus with metadata like language, date and source. Step 3 shows the corpus cleaned and, if needed, annotated with labels such as sentiment or entity tags. Step 4 shows three uses of the prepared corpus: analysing language patterns, training a system, and testing system performance. The main idea is that a corpus starts as collected language material and becomes useful after organisation and sometimes labelling.
visual.reducedMotionDescription: A static four-column flowchart shows the same stages without animation: source texts, corpus collection, cleaned and annotated corpus, and use for analysis, training or testing.

workedExample.scenario: A team wants a simple system to detect whether public transport comments are complaints or not.
workedExample.input: 8,000 short comments in English and Spanish from city feedback forms, with 6,000 labelled for training and 2,000 held back for testing.
process: Collect comments and basic metadata such as language and date.
Remove duplicates, fix broken text encoding, and separate English from Spanish.
Human reviewers label each comment as “complaint” or “not complaint”.
Use the labelled corpus to train a text classifier and then test it on the 2,000 held-back comments.
workedExample.result: The output is a trained classifier plus evaluation results, for example showing stronger performance on English than Spanish, which tells the team the Spanish part of the corpus may need expansion or better labels.

unWorkplaceExample.scenario: After a disaster, a UN team wants to analyse large volumes of incoming situation reports, logistics updates and public bulletins in several languages to identify recurring needs and locations mentioned.
unWorkplaceExample.relevance: A corpus of approved, relevant texts can be assembled and annotated to support named-entity recognition, topic modelling or summarisation for internal analysis. The key point is that the corpus is the organised language collection used for those tasks, not the task itself.
unWorkplaceExample.caution: Do not place confidential operational reports, personal data, survivor testimonies, protection-sensitive details or security-sensitive information into an unapproved public AI service when building or analysing a corpus; follow approved data-protection and information-security procedures.

whyItMatters: If you commission, buy, evaluate or govern an AI language system, you need to ask what corpus it was built and tested on. That affects what language varieties it handles, what biases it may repeat, and whether results fit your context. A system trained on news text may fail on field reports. A corpus with only major languages may exclude low-resource languages. Knowing about corpora helps you ask practical questions about coverage, quality, consent, labelling, and representativeness before relying on outputs.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: A corpus is just any dataset.
commonMisconceptions.correction: A corpus is a kind of dataset, but the term usually points to a collection of language material such as text or transcripts. A dataset can contain many other things, including images, sensor readings or mixed data types.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: A bigger corpus always means a better system.
commonMisconceptions.correction: Size helps only if the content fits the task and is of usable quality. A very large corpus with noisy text, weak labels or the wrong domain can perform worse than a smaller, carefully chosen corpus.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: A corpus is the same as a knowledge base.
commonMisconceptions.correction: A corpus stores examples of language as people wrote or said it. A knowledge base stores structured facts or records designed for retrieval. Some systems use both, but they serve different roles.

simpleVsTechnical.simple: A corpus is a large organised collection of language examples that people use to study language or build and test language tools.
simpleVsTechnical.technical: In language technology, a corpus is a curated collection of textual or transcribed linguistic data, often stored with metadata and sometimes with annotations such as part-of-speech tags, entity labels, sentiment labels or aligned translations. It may be monolingual, multilingual or parallel, depending on the task. A corpus can be used for descriptive analysis, feature extraction, supervised or unsupervised model development, and evaluation. The term is narrower than dataset because it usually refers specifically to language material rather than arbitrary data, and narrower than knowledge base because it typically contains observed language instances rather than normalised factual assertions.

keyTakeaway: A corpus is the organised language material behind many language AI systems, so its quality and coverage strongly shape what those systems can and cannot do.

quickCheck.question: Which description best matches a corpus in language technology?
options: A database of verified facts about the world stored as structured records
A collection of texts or transcripts organised for analysing language or training and testing language tools
A single very long document used to prompt a chatbot
A list of image files with bounding boxes for object detection
quickCheck.explanation: A corpus is a collection of language material such as texts or transcripts, usually organised for a purpose like analysis, training or evaluation. A knowledge base stores structured facts, a prompt is just input text, and image files for object detection are a different kind of dataset.
